title: Midas aureus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Bacchus leaves the fields and goes with a better company to the vineyards of Tmolus and to the Pactolus, a river that at this time was not golden. Silenus, missing from the god's train, is caught reeling by Phrygian country people and brought garlanded to their king, Midas, who keeps festival for him ten days and ten nights before returning him; the god repays the kindness by letting the king name any gift he likes, and the king asks that whatever he touches with his body turn to gold. Twig, stone, clod, grain, fruit, doorpost and washing-water all obey, until the food and drink at his own table turn to metal in his mouth and he begs the god to take the gift back. Bacchus sends him to bathe at the river's source near Sardis, and the part closes with the fields along that water still stiff and pale with gold.

sentences.t: Nec satis hoc Baccho est:
sentences.l: Nor is this enough for Bacchus:
sentences.i: But this is not enough for Bacchus:
sentences.n: Baccho is a dative where English wants a preposition: the Latin says “this is not enough to Bacchus”. The demonstrative hoc points back to something that happened before line 85; whatever it names is not in these lines, so the sentence opens by looking over its own shoulder.

sentences.t:
ipsos quoque deserit agros
cumque choro meliore sui vineta Timoli
Pactolonque petit, quamvis non aureus illo
tempore nec caris erat invidiosus harenis.
sentences.l: he leaves the fields themselves as well, and with a better troupe seeks the vineyards of his own Timolus and the Pactolus — although at that time it was not golden, nor enviable for its precious sands.
sentences.i: he abandons the countryside itself as well, and with a better company makes for the vineyards of his own Tmolus and for the Pactolus — though at that time the river was not golden, and nobody envied it its precious sand.
sentences.n: Pactolon keeps its Greek accusative ending in -on; the edition spells the mountain Timoli (Tmolus). Invidiosus takes the ablative caris harenis, “enviable on account of its precious sands”. The clause is planted for later: lines 142–145 of this same part tell how the gold came into this water and into the ground beside it, so the ending is announced before the story starts.

sentences.t:
Hunc adsueta cohors satyri bacchaeque frequentant,
at Silenus abest:
sentences.l: This river the accustomed throng, satyrs and bacchants, crowd, but Silenus is missing:
sentences.i: The usual retinue, satyrs and bacchants, throng the river; but Silenus is not there:
sentences.n: The subject is the singular cohors, “throng”, but the verb frequentant is plural, pulled into agreement by the plural nouns satyri and bacchae set beside it — agreement with the sense rather than the form. Hunc is the river, picked up from the Pactolon of line 87. Magnus prints adsueta with the unassimilated ads-, and that spelling is kept here rather than normalised to ass-.

sentences.t:
titubantem annisque meroque
ruricolae cepere Phryges vinctumque coronis
ad regem duxere Midan, cui Thracius Orpheus
orgia tradiderat cum Cecropio Eumolpo.
sentences.l: him, staggering with both his years and neat wine, country-dwelling Phrygians took, and, bound with garlands, led him to king Midas, to whom Thracian Orpheus had handed down the secret rites together with Cecropian Eumolpus.
sentences.i: Phrygian farmers caught him reeling with age and neat wine, tied him up with garlands and brought him to their king, Midas — the man to whom Thracian Orpheus, along with Eumolpus of Athens, had passed on the mysteries.
sentences.n: Cepere and duxere are the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere for -erunt; the ending says nothing about tense or voice, and it comes back in this part at posuere, line 119. Merum is wine unmixed with water, so titubantem annisque meroque gives two causes for one stagger. Cecropius means Athenian, from Cecrops, the first king of Athens; Midan keeps a Greek accusative.

sentences.t:
Quem simul agnovit socium comitemque sacrorum,
hospitis adventu festum genialiter egit
per bis quinque dies et iunctas ordine noctes.
sentences.l: And as soon as he recognised him as an associate and companion of the rites, he kept festival merrily at the arrival of his guest through twice five days and the nights joined on in their order.
sentences.i: The moment he recognised him as a fellow in the rites and a companion of them, he threw a festival for his guest's arrival and kept it up for ten days and the ten nights that ran on with them.
sentences.n: Quem is a connecting relative — a relative pronoun standing where English starts a new sentence, so “and him” rather than “whom”. Simul here is short for simul ac, “as soon as”. Bis quinque, “twice five”, is the poem's way of writing ten; the number is a flourish, not a difficulty. Magnus prints Quem, the object of agnovit; some editions print qui, which makes the relative the subject instead.

sentences.t:
Et iam stellarum sublime coegerat agmen
Lucifer undecimus, Lydos cum laetus in agros
rex venit et iuveni Silenum reddit alumno.
sentences.l: And already the eleventh Light-bringer had driven together the lofty column of the stars, when the king comes glad into the Lydian fields and gives Silenus back to his young foster-son.
sentences.i: The eleventh morning star had already herded the high parade of stars away, when the king came happily into the fields of Lydia and gave Silenus back to the young god the old man had reared.
sentences.n: Lucifer is the Light-bringer, the morning star; the eleventh of them counts off the ten days and nights just described. Cogere agmen is a military phrase — to drive a column together, and so to bring up its rear — which is why the literal keeps the plain “driven together”: the last star out marshals the rest off the sky. Reddit is a present standing in a past narrative (the historic present) beside the pluperfect coegerat, which is why the two layers here differ in tense. Alumnus is the nursling or foster-child: the young god was reared by Silenus, so the pupil receives his own teacher back.

sentences.t:
Huic deus optandi gratum, sed inutile, fecit
muneris arbitrium, gaudens altore recepto.
sentences.l: To him the god made the choice of a gift to be wished for — welcome, but useless — rejoicing in his foster-father recovered.
sentences.i: The god, glad to have his old guardian back, gave him the choice of any gift he wanted — a welcome choice, and a useless one.
sentences.n: Optandi muneris is a gerundive phrase, “of a gift to be wished for”, and arbitrium is the free power of decision: the god hands over the choosing itself. Gratum and inutile agree with arbitrium and are the poet's verdict, delivered before the wish is even spoken. Altore recepto is not an ablative absolute: gaudeo governs an ablative of its own, so the phrase is what he rejoices in, with recepto a participle agreeing with altore.

sentences.t:
Ille male usurus donis ait “effice, quidquid
corpore contigero fulvum vertatur in aurum.”
sentences.l: He, going to make bad use of the gifts, says: “Bring it about that whatever I shall have touched with my body be turned into tawny gold.”
sentences.i: He, who would put the gift to bad use, said: “Make whatever I touch with my body turn to yellow gold.”
sentences.n: Usurus is a future participle and utor takes the ablative donis: “about to use the gifts badly”. Effice governs vertatur directly, with no ut — a bare subjunctive of command after a verb of effecting. Contigero is a future perfect, “shall have touched”, which the literal keeps and natural English drops. The fatal word is corpore, “with my body”, not manu, “with my hand”: at lines 123–126 the mouth and teeth are body too.

sentences.t:
Adnuit optatis nocituraque munera solvit
Liber, et indoluit, quod non meliora petisset.
sentences.l: Liber nodded to the things wished and paid out the gifts that were going to do harm, and grieved that he had not asked for better things.
sentences.i: Liber agreed to the wish and paid over a gift that would do harm, sorry the man had not asked for better.
sentences.n: Liber is an Italian god long since identified with Bacchus, so the name changes but the god does not. Adnuit takes the dative optatis, literally “nodded to the things wished for”. Nocitura is a future active participle, “going to do harm” — the harm is not yet done. Solvit here is the language of paying out or discharging what is owed; the same verb comes back at line 135 with the opposite result, releasing the gift instead of handing it over. Quod with the subjunctive petisset (a shortened petivisset) gives the reason as the god's own thought. The second witness does not carry line 105 at all; Magnus prints it, and with it the god's regret.

sentences.t:
Laetus abit gaudetque malo Berecyntius heros
pollicitique fidem tangendo singula temptat
sentences.l: Glad, the Berecyntian hero goes away and rejoices in the harm, and tests the good faith of the promise by touching things one by one
sentences.i: The Berecyntian hero goes off happy, glad of his own harm, and tests whether the promise holds by touching things one at a time
sentences.n: Berecyntius means Phrygian, from Mount Berecyntus in Phrygia. Malo is the poet's word, not the king's: the man thinks he is rejoicing in a gift and the line calls the thing an evil. Polliciti is the perfect participle used as a noun, “the thing promised”, and tangendo is a gerund in the ablative, “by touching”. As printed here, line 107 ends with no punctuation at all and line 108 begins with a capital V; those two lines are what was checked. The clause at 107 is complete and the sense requires a full stop there, but nothing has been altered.

sentences.t:
Vixque sibi credens non alta fronde virentem
ilice detraxit virgam: virga aurea facta est.
sentences.l: And scarcely believing himself, from a holm-oak that was not tall he pulled a twig green with leaves: the twig was made gold.
sentences.i: Hardly believing his own senses, he pulled a green twig from a low holm-oak: the twig turned to gold.
sentences.n: Non alta is ablative and can attach either to fronde, “green with foliage that is not high”, or to ilice, “from a holm-oak that is not tall”; both nouns are ablative and the word order does not settle it. The literal here takes it with ilice. Facta est is the passive of facio doing the work English gives to “become”. Notice the pattern that now begins: the noun on one side of the colon is picked up on the other — virgam and virga here, saxum and saxum at 110, glaebam and glaeba at 111.

sentences.t: Tollit humo saxum: saxum quoque palluit auro.
sentences.l: He lifts a stone from the ground: the stone too grew pale with gold.
sentences.i: He picks a stone up off the ground: that stone too went pale with gold.
sentences.n: Humo is a bare ablative of separation, “from the ground”, with no preposition — normal for this noun. Quoque here is the plain adverb “also”; watch it, because the same letters can be quo-que, “and with which”, and it does catch readers out. Palleo is to grow pale or wan, a verb at home in fear; here it is used of the whitish yellow of gold. The tenses jolt: present tollit against perfect palluit.

sentences.t:
Contigit et glaebam: contactu glaeba potenti
massa fit.
sentences.l: He touched a clod as well: at the powerful contact the clod becomes a lump of metal.
sentences.i: He touched a clod of earth too: under that potent touch the clod becomes an ingot.
sentences.n: Et here is not “and” but the adverb “too, even”, standing after its verb. Contactu potenti is an ablative of means, with potenti the i-stem ablative of potens. Massa is a lump or ingot of metal, so the whole change is in that one noun: earth goes in, bullion comes out. Perfect contigit gives way to present fit inside one sentence.

sentences.t:
Arentes Cereris decerpsit aristas:
aurea messis erat.
sentences.l: He plucked the dry ears of Ceres: the harvest was golden.
sentences.i: He picked dry ears of corn: the crop was gold.
sentences.n: Ceres stands for her own grain — the goddess named where we would name the crop. The same move returns at lines 121–122, where Cerealia munera are simply food. Arentes describes ripe corn as dried out rather than withered. Magnus prints the accusative plural Arentes; some editions print arentis, the same case in an older spelling.

sentences.t:
Demptum tenet arbore pomum:
Hesperidas donasse putes.
sentences.l: He holds an apple taken from a tree: you would think the Hesperides had given it.
sentences.i: He holds a fruit picked from a tree: you would think the Hesperides had made him a present of it.
sentences.n: Arbore is an ablative of separation without a preposition, “from a tree”. Putes is a potential subjunctive in the indefinite second person — the poem turning to you, the reader, and telling you what you would think; the same address returns at line 126 with videres. Donasse is a shortened donavisse. The Hesperides kept a garden of golden apples at the western edge of the world, which is the whole point of the comparison: the fruit in his hand looks like theirs.

sentences.t:
Si postibus altis
admovit digitos, postes radiare videntur.
sentences.l: If he has moved his fingers to the high door-posts, the door-posts seem to shoot out rays.
sentences.i: Whenever he lays his fingers on the tall doorposts, the doorposts look as though they are giving off rays of light.
sentences.n: A perfect indicative (admovit) in the if-clause with a present in the main clause makes this a general, repeated condition: not “if he once did” but “whenever he does”. Admoveo takes the dative postibus. Radiare is to send out rays, the verb built on radius, a spoke or beam. The next sentence builds the same repeated action with ubi and the pluperfect laverat.

sentences.t:
Ille etiam liquidis palmas ubi laverat undis,
unda fluens palmis Danaen eludere posset.
sentences.l: When he had even washed his palms in clear waters, the water flowing from his palms could have deceived Danae.
sentences.i: When he washed his hands in clear water, the stream running off his palms could have taken in Danae.
sentences.n: The conjunction ubi is held back to the fifth word of line 116, so the subordinate clause has already begun before its own connecting word arrives: Ille, etiam, liquidis, palmas, ubi. Posset is a past potential subjunctive, “could have deceived”. Danae was shut away and reached by Jupiter in the form of a shower of gold; the run-off from these hands looks so much like that shower that it could have fooled the one person who saw the real thing.

sentences.t:
Vix spes ipse suas animo capit aurea fingens
omnia.
sentences.l: Scarcely does he himself take his own hopes into his mind, shaping all things golden.
sentences.i: He can hardly take in his own hopes, picturing everything gold.
sentences.n: Capit animo is “takes into the mind”, the idiom for containing a thought. Fingens is to mould or shape, the sculptor's verb, used of imagining. The adjective aurea stands second from the end of line 118 and its noun omnia opens line 119, so the phrase “all things golden” is split across the line-break with the participle between — the sentence spills over exactly as the man's thoughts do.

sentences.t:
Gaudenti mensas posuere ministri
exstructas dapibus nec tostae frugis egentes.
sentences.l: For him rejoicing the servants set out tables piled with feasts and not lacking roasted grain.
sentences.i: The servants set out tables in front of him as he sat there delighted, heaped with dishes and not short of roasted grain.
sentences.n: Posuere is again the poetic perfect in -ere for -erunt. Gaudenti is a participle standing alone as a noun in the dative — the man is identified here only by his mood, “for the one rejoicing”. Egeo takes the genitive frugis. Nec egentes is a real understatement in the Latin, “not lacking”, and both layers keep it rather than flattening it to “full of”.

sentences.t:
Tum vero, sive ille sua Cerealia dextra
munera contigerat, Cerealia dona rigebant,
sive dapes avido convellere dente parabat,
lammina fulva dapes admoto dente premebat.
sentences.l: Then indeed, whether he had touched the gifts of Ceres with his own right hand, the gifts of Ceres grew stiff; or whether he was making ready to tear the food apart with a greedy tooth, a tawny sheet of metal pressed down on the food as the tooth was brought near.
sentences.i: Then in earnest: if he touched the gifts of Ceres with his right hand, the gifts of Ceres went rigid; if he made to tear at his food with a greedy tooth, a sheet of yellow metal closed down over the food as the tooth came near.
sentences.n: Sive … sive with the indicative sets out two real alternatives, not two guesses. Cerealia munera, split across lines 121 and 122, becomes Cerealia dona later in 122: the poem says the same thing twice in different words, which is variation rather than a new idea. Admoto dente is a true ablative absolute — the tooth is not the subject or object of premebat — and English wants a clause for it, which is what both layers give. The edition spells the sheet lammina, with the doubled m, for the more familiar lamina, “a thin plate of metal”.

sentences.t:
Miscuerat puris auctorem muneris undis:
fusile per rictus aurum fluitare videres.
sentences.l: He had mixed the author of the gift with pure waters: you would have seen molten gold flowing through his gaping jaws.
sentences.i: He had mixed the giver of the gift into clear water: you would have seen molten gold streaming through his open jaws.
sentences.n: Auctorem muneris is the god named for his own product: Bacchus stands for the wine, so “mixing the giver of the gift with water” means watering the wine. The joke is bitter, since he gave both the wine and the curse. Rictus is the gape of an open mouth, a word ordinarily used of an animal's jaws. Videres is the past potential in the indefinite second person, “you would have seen”, matching putes at line 114.

sentences.t:
Attonitus novitate mali, divesque miserque,
effugere optat opes et, quae modo voverat, odit.
sentences.l: Thunderstruck by the strangeness of the evil, both rich and wretched, he longs to escape his riches and hates the things he had just now prayed for.
sentences.i: Stunned by the strangeness of the disaster, rich and miserable at once, he longs to get away from his wealth and hates what he had just been praying for.
sentences.n: Attonitus is literally “thunderstruck”, and novitate is an ablative of cause. Divesque miserque yokes the two words with the doubled -que, “both … and”, so that the pair have to be read against each other. Optat here belongs to a chain running through the whole episode: optandi at 100, optatis at 104, optat here, male optato at 136 — the verb of wishing keeps returning as the wish keeps costing more.

sentences.t:
Copia nulla famem relevat; sitis arida guttur
urit, et inviso meritus torquetur ab auro
sentences.l: No abundance relieves his hunger; dry thirst burns his throat, and, having earned it, he is tortured by the gold he hates
sentences.i: No amount of plenty takes his hunger away; parched thirst burns his throat, and he has earned it — he is tortured by the gold he loathes
sentences.n: Meritus is the perfect participle of the deponent mereor, so it is active in sense however passive it looks: “having deserved it”, not “deserved”. The literal keeps that active force. Invisus here is the one from invideo, “hated”, not a form meaning “unseen”. Torquetur with ab auro treats the metal as an agent, as if the gold were doing the torturing itself. As printed, line 130 ends with no punctuation and line 131 begins with a capital A; those two lines are what was checked. The clause at 130 is complete and the sense requires a stop there, but nothing has been altered.

sentences.t:
Ad caelumque manus et splendida bracchia tollens
“da veniam, Lenaee pater! peccavimus,” inquit,
“sed miserere, precor, speciosoque eripe damno.”
sentences.l: And raising his hands and gleaming arms to the sky, “Grant pardon, father Lenaeus! We have done wrong,” he says, “but have mercy, I beg, and snatch me from this handsome loss.”
sentences.i: And lifting his hands and shining arms to the sky he said: “Forgive me, father Lenaeus! I have done wrong — but have pity, I beg you, and pull me out of this beautiful ruin.”
sentences.n: Lenaeus is a cult title of Bacchus, from the Greek word for the wine-vat, so the god is addressed by the name that belongs to his press. Peccavimus is a first-person plural spoken by one man; the literal keeps the “we”, the idiomatic gives the “I” an English speaker would use. Splendida is the sting of the line: his own arms are shining, and at line 136 the god calls him circumlitus auro, smeared round with gold, while at 143 the golden power goes out of his body. Eripe takes an ablative of separation, damno, and speciosum damnum sets the two words at war — a loss that is a fine thing to look at.

sentences.t:
Mite deum numen: Bacchus peccasse fatentem
restituit factique fide data munera solvit
sentences.l: Mild is the divine power of the gods: Bacchus restores the man confessing that he has done wrong, and by the good faith of the deed releases the gifts that had been given
sentences.i: The gods have a mild power: Bacchus restores the man who admits he did wrong, and, good to his word in deed as well, undoes the gift he had made
sentences.n: Deum is the old short genitive plural for deorum, “of the gods”; it is a form, not a different word. The opening clause has no verb — “mild the divine power of the gods” — with est left to be understood; the finite verbs restituit and solvit belong to what follows the colon. Fatentem is the participle of the deponent fateor and is active in sense, “confessing”, which is how the literal takes it; peccasse (shortened peccavisse) throws the king's own peccavimus of line 132 back at him. Solvit is the same verb used at line 104 for handing the gift over, and it now means letting it go. Magnus prints factique, “of the deed”; some editions print pacti, “of the compact”, which makes the god faithful to his bargain rather than to his act. As printed, line 135 ends with no punctuation and line 136 opens with a quotation mark and a capital N; those two lines are what was checked. The clause at 135 is complete and the sense requires a stop there, but nothing has been altered.

sentences.t:
“Neve male optato maneas circumlitus auro,
vade”
sentences.l: “And so that you may not stay smeared round with the badly wished-for gold, go”
sentences.i: “And so you do not stay plastered over with gold you were wrong to wish for, go”
sentences.n: Neve is the negative form of the wish-and-command construction and takes the subjunctive maneas; the clause states the purpose of the imperative vade that comes after it, which is why English wants “so that you may not stay”. Male optato is the last link in the chain of wishing-words that began at line 100, and the adverb male passes judgement on the wish. Circumlino is to daub or plaster over: the participle makes the gold a coating on him rather than a possession. Magnus prints Neve; the second witness divides it as two words.

sentences.t:
ait “ad magnis vicinum Sardibus amnem
perque iugum ripae labentibus obvius undis
carpe viam, donec venias ad fluminis ortus,
spumigeroque tuum fonti, qua plurimus exit,
subde caput corpusque simul, simul elue crimen.”
sentences.l: he says, “make your way to the river neighbouring on great Sardis, and along the ridge of the bank, facing the gliding waters, until you come to the risings of the stream; and to the foam-bearing spring, where it comes forth at its fullest, put your head under, and your body at the same time, and at the same time wash off your guilt.”
sentences.i: he said. “Make for the river next to great Sardis, and take the crest of its bank, going against the current, until you reach the water's source; and where the foaming spring wells up at its fullest, put your head under it, and your body with it, and wash your guilt away at the same time.”
sentences.n: Vicinum takes the dative Sardibus; Sardis was the chief city of Lydia. Obvius with the dative labentibus undis means facing the gliding water, that is walking upstream. Donec with the subjunctive venias looks forward to an event not yet reached, “until you come”. Plurimus is nominative and agrees with the subject of exit, so it describes the spring at its fullest flow, not the water in some other way. Spumiger is a compound adjective, “foam-bearing”. The doubled simul at line 141 puts head, body and guilt into a single movement: the body goes under and the guilt comes off in the one act. Magnus prints iugum ripae, “the ridge of the bank”; some editions print nitens, which makes the traveller strain up the ridge instead.

sentences.t:
Rex iussae succedit aquae: vis aurea tinxit
flumen et humano de corpore cessit in amnem.
sentences.l: The king goes beneath the ordered water: the golden power dyed the river and passed out of the human body into the stream.
sentences.i: The king steps down under the water he had been told to enter: the power of gold stained the river and went out of his human body into the current.
sentences.n: Succedo takes the dative aquae and means going in under, not merely approaching. Iussae is transferred: the water was not ordered, the man was, and Latin lets the participle sit on the wrong noun in a way English cannot copy without unpacking it. Tingo is the verb for dipping cloth in dye, so the river is not merely coloured but dyed. Cessit, “withdrew, gave way”, treats the vis aurea as a thing that can move house.

sentences.t:
Nunc quoque iam veteris percepto semine venae
arva rigent auro madidis pallentia glaebis.
sentences.l: Now too, the seed of the old vein having been taken in, the fields stand stiff with gold, pale with their soaking clods.
sentences.i: Even now, with the seed of that old vein absorbed, the fields are hard with gold, pale where the clods lie soaked.
sentences.n: Percepto semine is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with the seed taken in” where English wants a clause. Vena is a vein of ore in the ground, and semen its seed, so the metal is spoken of as something sown. Three words here reach back into the part: rigent repeats the rigebant of line 122, where it was his food that stiffened; pallentia repeats the palluit of line 110; and glaebis repeats the glaeba of line 111. The stiffening and the pallor that were his affliction have become a property of the soil. And the whole closes the ring opened at lines 87–88, where the Pactolus was said not to be golden at that time.
